[38;5;231m●[39m The lighthouse stood on the last rock before the open water, a tower of grey stone that the sea had been trying to
  wear down for a hundred and twelve years. Its keeper was a woman named Maren Holt, who had come to the island at
  twenty-six, when her father's knees gave out and the Northern Lights Board needed someone willing to live on a rock
  with nothing but gulls for company. She had expected to stay two winters. She stayed thirty-one years.

  The island was called Sorrow by the fishermen, though the charts gave it a gentler name that nobody used. It was
  perhaps four hundred yards long and two hundred wide at its broadest, a hump of black basalt with a skin of thin grass
  and a few stubborn shrubs bent flat by the wind. There was a keeper's cottage, a storehouse, a small stone shed for
  the generator, and the tower itself, which rose from the highest point like a finger held up to say be careful. A
  landing stage of creosoted timber ran down to a cove on the leeward side, and in calm weather a boat could come in
  from the mainland, three miles off, to bring post and paraffin and sometimes a relief keeper. In winter the boat came
  rarely. In storms it did not come at all.

  Maren kept the light by habit more than by duty. Every evening at dusk she climbed the one hundred and six iron steps,
  checked the wick, trimmed the lamp, polished the great lens until she could see her own face in it, and wound the
  clockwork that turned the lantern. Then she wrote the entry in the logbook. Wind from the northwest, force five.
  Visibility good. Sea moderate. One vessel passed to the east, bound south, lights correct. The logbook was a record
  kept for the Board, but she had come to think of it as a letter addressed to nobody in particular, a way of saying
  here I am, here is the weather, here is the world as it looked from the top of the tower tonight.

  In her first years she had been lonely in a way she did not have words for. She talked to the gulls. She talked to the
  lens. She sang old songs her mother had taught her, badly, into the wind, and the wind carried them away without
  comment. Later the loneliness settled into something quieter, a companion
